meta_description: Food safety programs already generate the records they need; the work is joining them. Dataq Software builds FSMA 204 traceability pipelines, recall simulation drills, cold-chain exception management, and supplier-compliance portals on the grocery estate you operate today.

blocks.x: Every grocery and food retail requirement — approved supplier files, FSMA 204 traceability, GFSI certificates, cold-chain logs, EM swab results, complaint records — already produces digital exhaust. The failure is not documentation; it is that the exhaust lives in binders, spreadsheets, vendor dashboards, and email, so a recall question costs days and an audit costs weeks. Dataq Software builds the decision layer on the estate you already run: traceability evidence chains, recall simulation drills against real data, cold-chain exception management, and supplier-compliance portals. Read-first on control systems, honest on feasibility, and priced against what the delta actually saves.

A grocery chain with four hundred stores produces more food-safety records in a week than its audit calendar will ever read. Receiving clerks capture lot numbers at the dock, refrigeration probes in dairy and meat cases write samples every few minutes, sanitation teams file environmental swab routes, third-party auditors leave scores behind, and customer care transcribes complaints with product codes attached. None of that exhaust is missing. What is missing is the layer that joins it — so the affected-lot answer for a romaine event takes two days of conference calls instead of one query, because the records live in seven systems that were never asked to cooperate.

The regulatory frame keeps raising the stakes on that join layer. FSMA 204, the FDA Food Traceability Rule, requires a traceability lot code and records of Critical Tracking Events with their Key Data Elements for items on the Food Traceability List, producible within 24 hours of an official request. GFSI schemes — BRCGS, SQF, FSSC 22000 — require approved supplier files, certificate currency, and closure evidence on non-conformances. Large retail buyers layer their own traceability and approval demands on top of what law requires. Each requirement is, in engineering terms, a data contract with a latency clause, and programs that operate their contracts as pipelines answer requests in an afternoon.

Dataq Software is an engineering firm that builds the data and decision layer on top of the estate a food business already operates. We do not replace the ERP, the WMS, the POS, or the vendor platforms that hold probe and lab data. We read from them, model the evidence they emit, and build the systems that make it queryable at recall speed. Our posture on control systems and plant-floor equipment is read-first: we mirror, we do not inject. And we are honest about feasibility — if a two-week baseline of your traceability data shows the delta is not real, we say so and stop.
Approved supplier programs: a compliance state you can query

An approved supplier program is structurally a state machine. A vendor enters at onboarding with a questionnaire, a GFSI certificate, a certificate of insurance, and allergen declarations; it sits in approved status while documents are current; and it must escalate or exit when a certificate lapses, a non-conformance opens, or a recall letter arrives. Most programs track this state in a spreadsheet that updates monthly, and the failure mode is well known: a supplier's SQF certificate expires in March, the purchase orders keep flowing, and the first signal is an auditor finding in September. The supplier approval file exists to prevent exactly that outcome, and as a binder it cannot.

We build the approved-supplier state as a live dataset joined to purchasing. The supplier master feeds onboarding status; documents arriving from a supplier portal are parsed for scheme, site, category scope, and expiry; purchasing volume joins so the system distinguishes a lapsed certificate on a top-five frozen category from one on a seasonal garnish line. Escalation routes to the buyer who owns the category, not to a shared inbox nobody watches. The result is an approval file that passes an audit and, more usefully, a purchasing operation that stops buying exposure without anyone noticing a change in their workflow.

Onboarding deserves the same treatment as renewal, because most approval files rot at the entrance. Intake — questionnaire, certificate upload, insurance certificate, allergen declaration, specification agreement — lands in the same state model, so a supplier exists in exactly one status with exactly one evidence set from day one. Buyer-side overrides remain possible and are logged: a documented exception with an expiry date and an owner is compliance; an undocumented one is a finding waiting for an auditor. The same model handles offboarding and re-approval after suspension, which is where spreadsheets quietly keep purchase eligibility open for vendors who should not be eligible at all.
GFSI certificates, insurance documents, and the expiry ledger

Certificate management looks trivial until you count the objects. A grocery chain running private-label produce, deli, bakery, and ready-meal programs tracks BRCGS, SQF, and FSSC 22000 certificates per supplier site; certificates of insurance with per-occurrence limits and additional-insured endorsements; allergen declarations and Letters of Guarantee that die quietly when a formula changes. Each document type carries different expiry semantics: GFSI certificates expire on a printed date; insurance certificates expire on a date but the coverage terms matter more than the date; LOGs have no expiry at all and lapse silently on reformulation. A flat expiry report hides all three distinctions at once.

items: Expiry ledger with scope

Every certificate is parsed into scheme, issuing body, site, category scope, and expiry date. The ledger answers scoped questions directly: which ready-meal co-packers hold an FSSC 22000 audit window that stays valid past next quarter's launch date, and which produce suppliers expire during peak season.
Purchasing-weighted alerting

Expiry alerts are ranked by annual spend and unit volume through the category, so a lapse on a top-five frozen line reaches its buyer weeks ahead while a niche garnish supplier sits in the normal renewal queue.
Insurance certificate intelligence

Certificates of insurance are parsed for limits, additional-insured language, and expiry. A renewal that drops an endorsement is flagged as a change event for review rather than silently filed as current.
Renewal workflow in the portal

Suppliers upload renewals to a portal that validates document type, extracts dates and scope, and updates compliance state directly — replacing the email-and-rename convention that quietly loses files between audits.

blocks.x: Supplier non-conformance and SCAR workflows that close the loop

A supplier corrective action request is a promise with a deadline. A non-conformance opens — an out-of-spec micro result, a foreign-material finding, a labeling error caught at receiving — the supplier commits to containment and corrective action, and the program must verify closure with evidence. In spreadsheet-driven programs SCARs open reliably and close unreliably. Verification is an email thread, evidence is a PDF nobody re-reads, effectiveness checks have no owner, and repeat offenders hide inside aggregate supplier scorecards until the pattern is old enough to be an audit finding. Nothing in the file distinguishes a first offense from a fifth, and nothing measures how long containment actually took.

The workflow we build treats a SCAR as a tracked object with phases — containment, root cause, corrective action, effectiveness verification — each with evidence requirements, owners, and dates. Repeat-offense detection joins SCAR history to commodity, site, and season, so a third foreign-material event at one co-packer within a year surfaces automatically instead of living in tribal memory. Receiving inspections feed the same object: a lot rejected at the dock against an agreed specification generates the SCAR record at intake rather than three weeks later in a monthly meeting. Effectiveness verification closes the loop with a re-check date and a named owner, which is precisely the artifact an auditor asks to see.
FSMA 204: KDEs, CTEs, and the 24-hour clock

The FDA Food Traceability Rule applies to entities that manufacture, process, pack, or hold items on the Food Traceability List — fresh leafy greens, fresh-cut produce, nut butters, soft and semi-soft cheeses, fresh and frozen seafood among them. Its mechanics are data mechanics. Each listed food carries a traceability lot code; Critical Tracking Events — growing, receiving, transforming, shipping — must be recorded with their Key Data Elements: who, what, where, when, and the lot codes entering and leaving the event. On an official request, records must be produced within 24 hours, and for many retail operations that means an electronic spreadsheet in the FDA template.

Retailers and distributors sit in the receiving-and-shipping middle of the chain, which makes CTE capture a systems problem rather than a policy memo. Receiving must capture the traceability lot code from the supplier's shipping event — often a GS1 label the dock never scans today. Shipping to stores and DC transfers must generate the outbound event. Fresh-cut processing must record transformation from input lots to output lots. We build the CTE pipeline against the existing receiving flow: dock scan or ASN capture of incoming traceability lot codes, transformation events where processing splits or combines lots, and a traceability lot registry that answers the 24-hour request as a query. The regulator's spreadsheet template becomes an export, not a fire drill.

What breaks without the pipeline is predictable. Receiving teams scan item codes but not traceability lot codes, so upstream links vanish at the dock. Distribution centers transfer stock without recording lot-level destinations, so distribution maps go dark past the first hop. Store systems keep item-level sales but never the lot, so pull lists become estimates. Fresh-cut operations transform lots in production records that never join the inventory lot model. Each is a capture contract, not a platform purchase — and the rule is about completeness and retrievability of records, not about buying a new system to satisfy it.
The 24-hour requirement is a latency service-level agreement on a query. Either the estate can run that query or it cannot; every other FSMA 204 decision follows from which answer is true.
GS1 EPCIS 2.0: the event grammar for the whole chain

EPCIS 2.0, the GS1 standard for supply chain event exchange, defines a small set of verbs — object, transformation, aggregation, and association events — that map cleanly onto food traceability: commissioning a traceability lot, receiving it, transforming it in fresh-cut, aggregating cases onto pallets, decommissioning at sale. Trading partners that speak EPCIS can exchange Critical Tracking Events without a custom mapping per partner, which is why retailer-specified traceability programs increasingly accept it as the interchange format between suppliers, distribution centers, and buyers. The standard also enforces a discipline worth having even when nobody demands it: every event names its business step, its location, its time, and the identifiers involved.

blocks.x: Mock recalls that stress the data, not the phone tree

Most mock recalls test the phone tree, not the data. A team assembles, pulls the binder, calls the distribution centers, and produces an affected-lot list whose completeness nobody can verify. The exercise passes, and the underlying gaps stay hidden until a real Class I event: receiving lot codes never captured, POS sales not linkable to lots, store inventory not traceable to the distribution center that shipped it, e-commerce orders invisible to the recall team entirely. A rehearsal that runs against production data finds those gaps in minutes, while they are still cheap to fix.

We run recall simulations as drills against live estate data. Pick a real lot from last quarter's receipts and ask the system for every downstream location, every store that received it, every POS transaction that sold it, and every open inventory unit still in a DC. The drill scores itself: reconciliation time, lot-capture coverage at receiving, the share of stores whose sales join to the lot, and the number of manual steps each answer required. The first drill on an unprepared estate is humbling, which is the point. Each subsequent drill measures the pipeline instead of the phone tree, and the improvement curve becomes the program's actual recall-readiness metric — one a board can read without translation.
A mock recall that produces a tidy report from binder data has tested nothing. The valuable artifact is the gap list the drill exposes — and the second drill that shows the gap list shrinking.
Recall execution: pull lists, DC holds, and the communication tree

When a recall is real, three artifacts decide how the day goes: the affected-lot identification that maps supplier lots to internal traceability lot codes and finished goods; the distribution map that names every DC, store, and downstream customer holding affected product; and the pull list that tells a store associate what to remove from the floor, how to log it, and what to scan out. Building those artifacts in hours instead of days is a data engineering outcome. It depends on joins built before the crisis and rehearsed while nothing was on fire.

items: Affected-lot expansion

Start from the supplier's recalled lots and expand through transformation events into finished-goods lots — a salsa recall becomes the prepared-food and deli lots that used it — then resolve to store-level delivery records and open inventory.
POS pull lists

Generate store-specific pull lists joined to POS item codes, with expected on-hand by store, scan-out procedure, and a reconciliation against sales that quantifies recovered product instead of guessing.
DC hold workflows

Place inventory holds in the WMS by lot, quarantine stock to designated locations, and track disposition — return, destruction, or donation under policy — with evidence attached for the regulatory file.
Regulator and partner notices

Assemble recall communications from the evidence chain — affected lots, distribution window, quantities, product identifiers — so regulatory notification and customer letters come from data rather than from memory under pressure.

blocks.x: Cold chain from DC dock to store shelf

Cold-chain data is abundant and poorly parented. Distribution center refrigeration, dock doors, and store cases produce temperature samples continuously; vendor dashboards show them behind per-vendor logins; and the exceptions that matter — a dairy case drifting above 41°F through a two-hour window, a reefer trailer unloading warm, a dock door propped open during a summer delivery — arrive as alerts into systems nobody owns. HACCP logs, meanwhile, remain paper in many stores: a clipboard walk twice a day, filed at month-end, invisible until an inspector asks for the last ninety days.

The exception-management layer we build parents every temperature stream to an asset, a store or DC, and a product-risk class, then routes excursions by consequence. A two-degree drift on a frozen case becomes a refrigeration work order. A four-hour excursion on a dairy case holding saleable product becomes a disposition decision with quarantine, product review, and a food-safety sign-off. HACCP log digitization covers what probes miss — manual checks, calibration records, corrective actions — in the same store application, so an inspector's request is one retrieval. Excursion history also joins to shrink and complaint data, which is where chronic case problems finally attract capital attention instead of another work order.
Date codes, FEFO, and the markdown curve on perishables

Perishable category management is a race between sell-through and date codes, and the data to run it exists in every ERP and POS — rarely in one place. FEFO discipline, first-expired-first-out, requires on-hand inventory by date code at store level. Markdown curves require knowing how sell-through responds to a discount at each days-from-expiry bucket, observed in your own stores rather than assumed from a deck. Shrink accounting requires separating known loss — markdown, donation, documented destruction — from unknown loss, the silent difference between book and physical. Most chains run all three on exports, weekly spreadsheets, and instinct.

We build the date-code decision layer on existing inventory and sales data: on-hand by expiry bucket per store per item, markdown recommendations by days-to-code using the category's own observed elasticity, and a shrink ledger that codes every disposition so known and unknown loss separate cleanly. The wins are concrete. A bakery category that learns it should mark down at day two rather than at closing recovers margin a flat policy burns every night. A produce category that shows unknown-loss concentration in a handful of stores gets one targeted audit team visit instead of a chain-wide survey. No new hardware is required; the event stream already exists in the POS and the inventory ledger.
Fresh categories: known loss, unknown loss, and the shrink ledger

Fresh-category shrink is where food retail's margin leaks, and where the distinction between known and unknown loss does all the work. Known loss is coded: markdown at the case, donation to a food bank under policy, documented destruction of spoiled product, returns to a distribution center. Unknown loss is the residue — book inventory minus physical count minus known dispositions — and it hides everything from scan errors at self-checkout to receiving short-ships to theft. A category can show healthy known-loss discipline and still bleed points of margin into unknown loss that nobody can locate.

We build the shrink ledger as a dataset rather than a report: every disposition coded, every count variance categorized, joined to store, department, item, date code, and — where the traceability registry exists — to receiving lots. Unknown-loss concentration then has coordinates. It points to the three stores whose receiving counts never match the ASN, the department whose markdowns are scanned as voids, the vendor whose pallets run short with suspicious consistency. The weekly fresh review reads that table in ten minutes, and the loss-prevention team stops surveying the chain and starts visiting locations. None of it requires new hardware; it requires that dispositions stop dying in a notebook at the back office.
Environmental monitoring: zone maps, swabs, and pathogen-positive follow-up

An environmental monitoring program in a fresh-cut plant or a DC ready-meals kitchen is a scheduled evidence pipeline: a zone map running from Zone 1 food-contact surfaces out to Zone 4 areas beyond the hygiene perimeter, a swab schedule weighted by zone and risk, laboratory results that return days later, and — when a pathogen-positive lands — a follow-up protocol of intensified sanitation, vector swabbing, re-sampling, and product disposition review. The program's integrity lives in its metadata: which zone, which site, which equipment, which corrective action followed. Lose the metadata and a positive result is only a red number on a lab portal.

We model EM programs as data. Swab points become located, zoned objects with sampling history; results join to corrective-action records; pathogen-positives trigger the documented follow-up sequence automatically, with owners and due dates attached. Trend views answer the question certification bodies actually ask — not whether a positive occurred, but what was done and how the program knows it worked. For multi-site programs the same model compares kitchens running the same menu: two sites with different Listeria-monitoring patterns under identical procedures is a findings conversation that finally has data behind it, and the zone map makes repeated positives on adjacent points visible as a spatial pattern rather than a list.
Store audits, pest documentation, and the checklist problem

Store-level food safety runs on checklists: corporate audit templates, third-party inspection reports, pest control service documentation, temperature logs, sanitation schedules. The documents are numerous and the insight is scarce. A district manager reviewing thirty audits a week reads scores, not patterns. Pest control reports arrive as PDFs with activity findings nobody aggregates. The same handwash sink, the same backroom sanitation gap, the same receiving-door discipline problem repeat across visits without a mechanism connecting them across time, stores, and inspectors. The audit calendar itself lives in a spreadsheet, so inspection coverage — which stores received a third-party visit this quarter and which received nothing — is yet another manual reconciliation.

Checklist digitization matters less for the form than for the joins. We build the audit data model so findings carry location, department, and a coded classification; pest documentation parses into service dates, activity findings, and device maps that trend by store; inspection results join to the store's cold-chain excursion history and shrink data. The district view then shows what scores hide: the store whose audit score is fine but whose case-excursion history is chronic, or the pest activity pattern that precedes a customer complaint. The audit program stops being a scorecard archive and becomes a targeting system for where the next visit actually earns its cost.
Complaint triage: from the 1-800 call to the lot code

Customer complaints are the cheapest surveillance network a food retailer owns and the least joined to everything else. A complaint about foreign material in a salad kit arrives with a product code, a store, a date, and often a lot code printed on the packaging — but the case system stores the narrative, not the join. Hand triage treats the ninth complaint about the same production week like the first, and the pattern that should have triggered a supplier conversation surfaces only in a quarterly report nobody reads. Care scripts capture the product code but have nowhere to put the lot code that actually matters.

The triage pipeline we build extracts structured signals at intake — product, lot or date code, store, symptom class — joins them to the traceability lot registry and to receipt and production records, and clusters complaints by lot, site, and time window. Clustering changes the decision, not just the reporting. A single complaint is a case. Five complaints resolving to one lot within a week is a quality signal with a production date and a supplier attached. A complaint pattern that overlaps an environmental-monitoring pathogen-positive in the same plant and window is an incident. Triage also routes upward correctly: supplier complaints opened with evidence attached close faster because the SCAR starts from data instead of a phone call.
Withdrawals versus recalls, allergens, and the communication tree

The vocabulary matters because the obligations differ. A market withdrawal removes product still under the firm's control — a DC pull before distribution completes. A recall reaches product already in commerce: stores, foodservice customers, consumers. A Class I recall involves a health-hazard determination and carries regulator-facing timing and reporting obligations. Retail programs also run their own withdrawals for quality issues that never become regulatory events. Each path has different evidence, timing, and communication requirements, and they get conflated in exactly the organizations whose data would make the distinction easy to operate.

The communication tree — who is notified, in what order, with what content — is a data product, not an org chart printed in the crisis binder. Supplier recalls propagate through it to category buyers, DCs, store operations, e-commerce fulfillment, and customer care with lot-level facts attached. Store-facing notices carry the pull list and scan-out procedure. Customer-care scripts carry the lot identifiers to match against complaint intake. We build notification trees as configured workflows over the evidence chain, with acknowledgment tracking: the system knows which stores opened the notice and which reconciled their scan-out, which is the difference between a recall that worked and one whose completeness is asserted rather than demonstrated.
Allergen communication trees

Allergen events compress the same machinery into a shorter fuse. An undeclared-allergen withdrawal requires the affected-lot answer, the distribution map, and the communication tree — plus one join the regular tree lacks: product-recipe lineage, so every SKU that shares a line, a rework batch, or a cross-contact window with the affected production run is identified before the notice ships. The recall notice that forgets the second SKU produced on the shared line is how companies turn a withdrawal into a second recall. Recipe and lineage data usually exists in PLM or specification systems; the join to lots and communications is what we build.
Retailer-specified traceability and the supplier portal

Beyond regulation, large retail buyers impose their own traceability requirements on suppliers: lot-level visibility into private-label supply, response windows for recall letters, certification currency by category, and increasingly participation in retail traceability initiatives that expect event-level data in standardized formats. Suppliers answer these demands through portals, spreadsheets, and email, and the retailer's compliance team reconciles the results by hand. The burden falls unevenly — the same supplier may serve five retailers with five different questionnaire formats — and the retailer rarely sees which of its own suppliers are the chronic exceptions.

We build the supplier-facing side as a portal that publishes one requirement set per category and accepts evidence in structured form: certificates parsed on upload, traceability data in EPCIS 2.0 or the retailer's template, and recall response acknowledgments tracked with timestamps. The compliance state — current, expiring, missing, chronically late — becomes a query joined to purchasing, which changes buyer behavior long before it changes audit outcomes. Suppliers benefit too, because one portal with parsed validation is faster than five email threads, and a document's receipt becomes provable rather than assumed.
The decision stack: from dock scan to recall answer

The reference architecture below lays out the decision stack for a grocery food-safety program: where records originate, how they are captured and normalized, where the evidence layer sits, which engines make program decisions, and what the response and audit surfaces consume. Everything in the first lane already exists in some form on the estate; the engineering work is ingestion contracts, the evidence model, and the engines that turn evidence into decisions. Note what is absent: no proposal to replace the ERP, WMS, POS, or probe vendor platforms. The stack reads from them, and control systems remain untouched.

blocks.x: How Dataq Software engages

Engagements begin against your own data, in your cloud account or on-premises environment, with a baseline that prices the delta before any build is approved. The two-week entry point is standard because it is the shortest interval over which an estate reveals its real capture behavior. Build decisions that follow are gated on what the baseline proves, sized to the joins it exposes, and delivered into your repository with runbooks your team owns. Nothing in the engagement requires replacing ERP, WMS, POS, or vendor probe platforms; the work connects them, and the connective tissue is where every hour of recall speed comes from.

items: Two-week traceability baseline

We ingest one quarter of receiving, shipping, and POS data, attempt the FSMA 204 affected-lot query end to end, and report lot-capture coverage at receiving, join gaps to stores, and time-to-answer — measured on your records, priced as a fixed engagement.
Recall simulation drill

One drill against production data with a scored report: affected-lot completeness, distribution-map accuracy, pull-list generation time, and the manual steps each answer required. The scorecard is the roadmap.
Supplier-compliance portal build
Certificate parsing, expiry ledger, renewal workflow, and SCAR tracking built on your ERP supplier master — one requirement set per category, parsed on upload, joined to purchasing.
Cold-chain exception layer
Probe streams parented to assets and product-risk classes, excursion routing by consequence, and HACCP digitization in the same store application your teams already open.
Honest stop condition

If the baseline shows traceability lot codes are simply not captured at receiving, the report says what capture change is required before any pipeline is worth building. We do not sell integration work that cannot answer recall questions.

blocks.x: Questions food safety leaders ask us

items: We already bought a food-safety platform. Why does recall response still take days?

Platforms excel at workflows — audits, checklists, document storage. Recall speed is a join problem across WMS, POS, supplier events, and transformation records, and most platforms treat those systems as someone else's estate. We build the join layer and the registry beneath your platform, and let it keep the workflows it is good at.
Can you work with our WMS and plant systems without touching them?

Yes. Our posture is read-first on control systems: we mirror event streams and records, and we do not inject into control paths. Where capture is missing — traceability lot codes at receiving, lot destinations on transfers — we propose the minimal change at the dock or ASN level, and your team owns the decision.
What does FSMA 204 actually require of a retailer?

Capture of receiving and shipping Critical Tracking Events with their Key Data Elements for foods on the Food Traceability List, maintenance of the traceability lot code through your distribution, and records producible within 24 hours of an official request — including an electronic spreadsheet in the FDA template. The engineering task is making that an export from a registry rather than a scramble.
How fast can a mock recall realistically get?

The first honest drill on an unprepared estate takes days and exposes the gaps — that is its value. After the registry and ingestion layer land, hours becomes the normal operating state, and each subsequent drill report shows the trend so readiness is a measured number rather than a claim.
Do we have to force every supplier onto a portal?

No. The portal works for suppliers who adopt it, and the parsing layer keeps working on what continues to arrive by email or PDF. The difference either way is that document acceptance becomes provable, expiries become queryable, and late responders become visible by name.
Who owns the data model after the engagement?

You do. Models, pipelines, and engines are delivered in your cloud account and your repository, with documentation and runbooks your team maintains. Dataq Software is hired for the delta, not for custody of your data.
What if our volume is too small for this to matter?

Then the baseline says so and we stop. A category with two suppliers and complete lot capture may need a workflow fix rather than a data program, and the two-week baseline exists to price that honestly before anyone builds anything.
How does this change the auditor conversation?

Audits stop being archaeology. Certificate currency, non-conformance closure, EM follow-up sequences, and the traceability query become retrievals with timestamps, which shortens fieldwork and removes the scramble. The same evidence serves certification bodies, customer audits, and the FDA request without reformatting three times.
